_: SEC-5 justified exceptions for tools/secret-scan.mjs. Each entry is a (file, key) pair, never a whole file, because allowlisting a file pre-authorizes every secret a later edit pastes into it. 'why' is mandatory and is the review surface: an entry whose reason does not survive reading is an entry to delete, not to keep. An entry matching nothing fails the scan, so this list cannot silently outlive what it exempts.

allow.why: CI harness fixture, not a secret: the SA password of an ephemeral SQL Server service container on the runner-private network, alive for one job and reachable by nothing outside it. It cannot be generated per run, because a service container's env is resolved at workflow parse time and cannot read a value a step produced.

CI harness fixture, not a secret: the connection string embedding the same ephemeral SA password allowlisted above. It is a second copy of that value rather than an independent one, which CFG-1 would object to if either were a committed configuration value rather than a workflow-local literal. It was keyed 'CS' until 2026-07-28, when the e2e job stopped re-implementing scripts/e2e.sh and started calling it (E-104); the variable is now named for what the script reads rather than for what the inline copy happened to call it.

Test harness fixture, not a secret: a symmetric signing key used only by the in-process architecture-test host, which serves no traffic and holds no data. It has to be a committed constant because the tests both mint and verify with it. Found by this mechanism's first run and never named in the findings register, which is why it is recorded as E-17 rather than quietly exempted here.

The value is the NAME of a configuration key, not a credential: `ConnectionStrings:Kernel` is the path at which the connection string is looked up, and the string itself resolves from user-secrets or the environment and is never committed. DB2 puts it here so the engine declaration says where its connection string lives, which is the opposite of putting the connection string here. The scan is right to fire on the key name, because a leaf called connectionStringKey usually does hold one; this is the reviewed exception SEC-5 asks for rather than a widening of the registry, which would blind the scan to every real connection string in the tree.
